statements: The study evaluated whether an author-compiled ophthalmic guideline table could provide all instance-level labels needed to train a multi-turn telephone triage agent.
The authors compiled American Academy of Ophthalmology-informed guidance into a 70-row operational triage table.
Each generated profile cited a nonempty rule-row set and inherited the most severe tier among the cited rows.
The primary training corpus contained 3,000 synthetic multi-turn dialogues with a median of 11 nurse turns.
The 3,000-dialogue corpus contained 625 emergent, 746 urgent, and 1,629 routine dialogues.
Class-weighted resampling with weights 2.0, 1.5, and 1.0 produced 3,998 training exposures.
The GAO-Triage intervention was full-parameter supervised fine-tuning of a 9B backbone for three epochs with nurse-token cross-entropy and caller-token masking.
The operational reference included 42 emergent, 47 urgent, and 112 routine cases.
Providing the 70-row rule table to GPT-5.5 yielded 67.7% agreement versus 75.1% without the table.
GAO-Triage achieved 74.1% exact agreement with the operational reference versus 61.7% for the untuned 9B backbone.
Among 42 emergent-reference cases, GAO-Triage recall was 69.0% versus 9.5% for the untuned 9B backbone.
Severe under-triage decreased descriptively from 24 cases with the base model to 17 cases with GAO-Triage.
A second same-recipe random seed achieved 73.1% agreement and 78.6% emergent recall.
Under a second patient simulator, emergent recall was 71.4% for GAO-Triage versus 7.1% for the base model.
Most comparisons relied on one random seed and one patient simulator, and the design was underpowered for paired differences below roughly 10 percentage points.
Permuting dialogue-label assignments collapsed the model to routine predictions for all 201 cases, with 55.7% agreement and 0% emergent and urgent recall.
Removing or replacing the 160 tagged one-fact boundary dialogues changed agreement by at most 2 of 201 cases.
Approximately 19% of earlier rationale fields asserted findings that the caller had not supplied.
Label repair neutralized 491 symptom-family/tier contradictions and corrected 91 dialogues with three mutually inconsistent labels.
Outcome-GRPO achieved 45.3% agreement and ended without a disposition in 80 of 201 dialogues.
Providing the 70-row rule table to GPT-5.5 yielded 67.7% agreement versus 75.1% without the table.
On Oxford-40, a trained precursor achieved 62.5% agreement, the untuned backbone 50.0%, and GPT-5.5 82.5%.
The 70-row operational policy was benchmark-informed, lacked independent clinician validation, and was not mapped to source passages.

The benchmark informed rule-table revision, corpus development, model selection, and reference adjudication, limiting the evaluation to policy conformance rather than held-out clinical generalization.
Historical evaluation runs were invalidated because a complete-profile heuristic could overwrite model verdicts using hidden case data.
An exact-template audit across 5,427 historical case-runs found 19 to 44 overwritten cases per run.
Most comparisons relied on one random seed and one patient simulator, and the design was underpowered for paired differences below roughly 10 percentage points.
Known paraphrase clusters and lexical-overlap findings did not establish isolation or decontamination of training data from benchmark content.
The external Oxford-40 test was small, static rather than interactive, used differing prompts, and had a 57.5% constant-emergent baseline.
The study retained no platform agreement, acquisition record, or de-identification audit for the public-post-derived data, and no IRB review was sought.
The authors concluded that guideline compilation can substitute for per-instance annotation for policy-conformance training when annotated conversations are scarce.
The authors stated that independent multi-clinician labels and an interactive external benchmark are prerequisites for a clinical claim.
